title: Cycling Route Planner: Bike Routes and GPX
description: Plan a cycling route between two places with the Cycling Route Planner — distance, ride-time estimate and GPX export for your device. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a cross-town ride routed on the cycling network usually runs a little longer than the driving route — the price of paths and quiet streets, shown before you set off.
quick_answer: The Cycling Route Planner finds a route between two locations on the cycling network — roads and paths a bicycle can actually use — and reports its distance and time. Review the route and export it as GPX for a bike computer or phone app when it looks right.
steps_intro: Cars get motorways; bikes get the interesting network. Plan on the right one:

Distance and shape first, café second. Export the GPX and the ride lives on your device, not in your memory of the map.
A tour is a chain of daily routes. Plan each leg here, check its distance against your daily range, and export the set before departure.
Visitors on hired bikes need legal, rideable routes, not local knowledge. The open network data stands in for the local friend.

A cycling route between two points often measures 5–15% longer than the same pair's driving route — the planner's number includes the path the law and the kerbs allow, which is the only number your legs will meet.
Export the planned route and it opens in standard bike apps and computers as a track to follow — the plan survives leaving the browser, which is the feature touring riders actually use.

faq: Does it prioritize protected bike lanes?

It routes on the bike-usable network the open data describes. Where the data records cycle infrastructure, the route can use it; the planner does not guarantee a protected lane the data does not know about.
Can I export the route?
Yes — GPX export is built in, for bike computers and the standard route apps. Plan here, ride there.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Cycling routes change with closures and works, not with traffic flow; the data snapshot is the limit, stated plainly.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Both road and path networks wind. The planner's distance is the ridden one — the only one your legs will meet.
Can route results change over time?
Yes, as the open map data improves: new paths appear, misclassifications get fixed. A route exported last season deserves a fresh look.
Can I add stops along the way?
Plan leg by leg: route to the stop, then from it. Each leg exports separately and chains on your device.
Does it avoid hills?
The planner reports the route the network gives; elevation strategy is the rider's — the hiking tools' Naismith thinking applies to legs too: climbs cost time whatever pulls you up them.
Can it plan a round trip loop?
Route out to a far point and back — or chain legs through waypoints by planning each leg. Loops assemble from legs here.
Are towpaths and trails included?
Where the open data maps them as rideable, yes. A path's legal status in data is a snapshot; local signs are the final law.
Why did it avoid the main road?
Because the cycling network prefers rideable links where the data offers them. The route optimises for bicycles, not for the shortest line a car would take.
